questions.question: A 48-year-old man comes to the OPD with complaints of excessive thirst, excessive micturition, and increased hunger. He also states that his skin colour has changed in the past six months. He is icteric on examination, and his skin examination reveals findings similar to those in the image below. What is the most likely cause of the change in his skin colour?

options.A: Excessive melanin production due to adrenal insufficiency
options.B: Excessive deposition of melanin and iron in the skin
options.D: Excessive deposition of bilirubin in the skin

explanation.text: The above patient has features of “ Bronze diabetes ” and liver dysfunction, which are typically seen in hemochromatosis. In Hemochromatosis, skin colour changes due to the deposition of excessive melanin >> iron in the skin. It is also known as "bronze diabetes" due to skin discolouration and associated pancreatic disease. The disease typically manifests after 20 g of stored iron has accumulated in the body.

Organs affected Clinical features Liver Hepatomegaly, elevated liver enzymes, risk of HCC Pancreas Iron induced damage of beta cells - diabetes mellitus Heart Cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, congestive heart failure Skin Hyperpigmentation - bronze skin due to melanin and iron deposition Joints Arthropathy and joint pain CNS Rarely - memory issues, depression and fatigue Hemochromatosis is of two types.

Types of hemochromatosis Features Hereditary hemochromatosis HFE -related: It is the classic form of hereditary hemochromatosis that is inherited in an autosomal recessive (chromosome 6p) HAMP gene mutation-related HJV gene mutation (juvenile hemochromatosis Acquired/secondary hemochromatosis Repeated blood transfusions Excessive oral intake or iron Excessive melanin production due to adrenal insufficiency ( Option A) is typically seen in Addison’s disease, where adrenal insufficiency leads to increased ACTH derived from Proopiomelanocortin, which also produces MSH and Endorphins, thus leading to melanogenesis, causing darkening of the skin and mucosal membranes Insulin resistance ( Option C) gives rise to Acanthosis Nigricans, which are hyperpigmented, velvety plaques typically found in body folds such as the neck, axillae, and groin.

It is also associated with gastric adenocarcinoma Bilirubin ( Option D) deposition leads to jaundice, characterized by a yellowish discoloration of the skin, not the bronze pigmentation seen in hemochromatosis. Jaundice is related to liver dysfunction or hemolysis, not iron overload

questions.question: A 38-year-old female presents with fatigue, joint pain, and bronze skin pigmentation. Labs show a heterozygous mutation in the HFE gene. The histopathology image is shown below. Which of the following is the best screening test for this condition?

options.D: Genetic testing for the HFE gene

explanation.text: The diagnosis in this case is hemochromatosis. Transferrin saturation (TSAT) is the best screening test for hereditary hemochromatosis. TSAT measures the amount of iron bound to transferrin, reflecting the body's iron status. Elevated TSAT levels (>45-50%) suggest iron overload, which is a characteristic feature of hemochromatosis. Serum ferritin is a protein that stores iron in the body.

However, while serum ferritin levels can be a useful indicator, they are not as specific as transferrin saturation (TSAT) for diagnosing hemochromatosis (Option A). In hereditary hemochromatosis, LFTs may show abnormalities in advanced stages of the disease when iron overload has caused liver damage (e.g., elevated alanine transaminase or AST levels).

**However, LFTs are not specific screening tests for hemochromatosis (Option C):** . Genetic testing for mutations in the HFE gene is the definitive diagnostic test for hereditary hemochromatosis (Option D).

questions.question: A 25-year-old patient presents with a history of tremors, dysarthria, and personality changes. Serum ceruloplasmin levels were found to be low. Based on the image below, what ocular finding is associated with the underlying condition?

explanation.text: The image shows characteristic Kayser-Fleischer rings, a brownish-green discolouration in the cornea. These rings are associated with Wilson's disease, a genetic disorder involving copper metabolism. Wilson's disease is a genetic disorder characterised by impaired copper metabolism. It leads to copper accumulation primarily in the liver, brain, and other organs.

Molecular genetic testing can identify mutations in the ATP7B gene, which is responsible for Wilson's disease. Clinical Features: Kayser-Fleischer Rings: These are characteristic brownish-green rings seen in the cornea due to copper deposition and are a hallmark feature of Wilson's disease. Serum copper is raised, while ceruloplasmin levels (a copper-binding protein) are decreased in Wilson's disease.

Increased urinary copper excretion is a characteristic finding in Wilson's disease. Arcus senilis refers to a white or greyish ring around the cornea that is commonly seen in elderly individuals. It is caused by lipid deposits in the peripheral cornea and is generally considered a normal age-related change. ( Option A) Roth spots are retinal haemorrhages with a white or pale centre.

Roth spots can be seen in various medical conditions, including bacterial endocarditis, leukemia, and diabetic retinopathy ( Option C) Horner's syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterised by a triad of eye and face symptoms. It includes ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid), miosis (constriction of the pupil), and anhidrosis (decreased sweating) on the affected side of the face ( Option D)

questions.question: Which of the following tests is the most specific for confirming the diagnosis of Wilson’s Disease?

explanation.text: Testing for Wilson's disease: Serum Ceruloplasmin (Option A): Low levels are suggestive.

**24-Hour Urinary Copper Excretion (Option B):** Increased in Wilson's disease Liver Function Tests (LFTs) (Option C): May show abnormalities. Kayser-Fleischer Rings Examination: Greenish-brown rings in the cornea. Genetic Testing: For ATP7B gene mutations, confirming diagnosis.
**Liver Biopsy (Option D):** Demonstrates hepatic copper accumulation (Most specific). Brain Imaging: MRI to assess neurological involvement.

questions.question: Which special stain is commonly used to aid in the diagnosis of Wilson's disease?

explanation.text: The Rubeanic acid stain, also known as the Rhodanine stain, is commonly used to detect copper accumulation in liver tissue, particularly in the hepatocytes' cytoplasmic granules. This stain forms a distinctive brown-black color when it reacts with copper, aiding in the diagnosis of Wilson's disease.

Rubeanic acid stain Stains the copper present within cytosolic granules of hepatocytes Oil red O stain Stains lipids (Option A) PAS stain Stains cells with high glycogen storage and also stains basement membrane (Option B) Prussian stain Stains hemosiderin / stored iron (Option D)

questions.question: A 50-year-old male presents with a history of chronic alcohol abuse and complains of right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, hepatomegaly is noted. Laboratory investigations show elevated liver enzymes. Gross feature of the liver has a characteristic mottled appearance. Based on these findings and the image below, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The patient's history of chronic alcohol abuse and the characteristic mottled appearance of the liver on imaging studies point towards Nutmeg Liver as the most likely diagnosis. Nutmeg liver, also known as congestive hepatopathy or passive hepatic congestion, is a condition characterized by a mottled appearance of the liver on imaging studies, resembling the cross-section of a nutmeg seed.

This appearance is due to centrilobular congestion and haemorrhage caused by chronic passive congestion of the liver, often secondary to right-sided heart failure, chronic venous congestion, or conditions leading to hepatic venous outflow obstruction.

Acute passive congestion (“nutmeg liver”). (A) The cut surface of the liver has a variegated mottled red appearance, representing congestion and haemorrhage in the centrilobular regions of the parenchyma. (B) On microscopic examination, the centrilobular region is suffused with red blood cells, and atrophied hepatocytes are not easily seen. Portal tracts and the periportal parenchyma are intact.

questions.question: A 25-year-old female presents with fatigue, jaundice, and abdominal pain. On examination, hepatomegaly is noted. Hepatocytes show globular inclusions which are strongly periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive. Her sibling died of the same liver condition a few years back. What is the primary function of the enzyme implicated in this condition?

explanation.text: Alpha-1 antitrypsin (α1AT) is a serine protease inhibitor that plays a crucial role in inhibiting proteases, particularly neutrophil elastase. Alpha-1 Antitrypsin ( α1AT ) deficiency is an autosomal recessive (AR) disorder with defective gene in Chromosome 14 - SERPINA1 gene In Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD), there is a deficiency or dysfunction of α1AT, leading to decreased inhibition of neutrophil elastase.

This results in uncontrolled protease activity, particularly neutrophil elastase, which can cause tissue damage, especially in the lungs and liver leading to pan-acinar emphysema and liver cirrhosis respectively Histopathology: The deficiency is characterised by the presence of round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes, which are strongly periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive and diastase-resistant.

questions.question: A 50-year-old patient with a history of recurrent biliary colic and cholangitis undergoes cholecystectomy. Multiple stones are retrieved intraoperatively, and an image of the stones is provided for reference. Which of the following is true about the type of pigmented stones likely seen in this patient?

explanation.text: The provided image and clinical scenario depicting black-pigmented stones retrieved during cholecystectomy.

**Feature Cholesterol Stones Pigment Stones Predisposing conditions Seen in Western populations (Option A):** , related to metabolic syndrome (Option B), obesity (Option D) and common in females Chronic hemolytic anaemia - Black stones Bacterial infections, parasitic infestations - Brown stones Composition >50% crystalline cholesterol monohydrate Calcium salts of unconjugated bilirubin and inorganic calcium salts Appearance Pale yellow, round to ovoid, granular, hard external surface Brown to black, soft, soap-like, spiculated or moulded contours Location Arise exclusively in the gallbladder Found in sterile gallbladder bile (black stones) or infected large bile ducts (brown stones) (Options C). Radiopacity Radiolucent (may become radiopaque with calcium carbonate) Black stones: 50-75% are radiopaque, Brown stones: Radiolucent

questions.question: All the following infections are associated with an increased risk of pigmented gallstones, except?

explanation.text: Aspergillus flavus plays a role in liver pathology primarily by producing aflatoxins. These are potent carcinogens that can cause liver damage, oxidative stress, and DNA mutations and ultimately increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. However, they are not associated with an increased risk of gallstones. Options A, B, and C are associated with pigmented gallstones.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not a complication associated with gallstones?

explanation.text: Complications of gallstones: Empyema Perforation Fistula formation Inflammation of the biliary tree (cholangitis) Obstructive cholestasis Pancreatitis (Option A) Gallstone ileus (Bouveret syndrome) (Option C) Increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma (Option B)

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents to the OPD with severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Clinical examination revealed a positive result for a clinical test shown in the image down below. An ultrasound of the abdomen shows an enlarged and tense gallbladder. Which of the following findings is most likely associated with this patient's condition?

explanation.text: Based on the provided clinical vignette and positive murphy sign, the patient's presentation aligns with acute cholecystitis. The most likely finding associated with this condition is subserosal hemorrhages.

Characteristics Acute cholecystitis Chronic cholecystitis Gall bladder appearance Thickened, tense, edematous, bright red or green-black Thickened, fibrotic, opaque grey-white Serosa Subserosal haemorrhages (Option D), fibrinopurulent exudate Smooth serosa with Subserosal fibrosis (Option C) (subepithelial fibrosis also seen) Histology Erosion of mucosa, Edema, congestion, sparse neutrophils Scattered lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages, fibrosis, Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses (Option B) Special forms Gallbladder empyema (pure pus), gangrenous cholecystitis, emphysematous cholecystitis Porcelain gallbladder, adenomyomatosis, Xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis (Option A), IgG4-related sclerosing cholecystitis, hydrops of the gallbladder

questions.question: Which condition is characterised by extensive dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall?

explanation.text: Porcelain gallbladder is characterized by extensive dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall. This condition is associated with chronic cholecystitis and may lead to an increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma.

**Porcelain gallbladder (Option A):** Hyalinizing cholecystitis (Option D) Characterized by extensive dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall. Characterized by complete replacement of the gallbladder wall and mucosa by dense fibrosis, with or without calcification. Associated with chronic cholecystitis and an increased risk of gallbladder carcinoma

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common benign tumor of the liver?

explanation.text: Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver Benign hepatic tumors: Cavernous hemangioma (most common) > focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) >hepatocellular adenoma (rare) Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign liver tumour. It appears as a discrete red-blue, soft nodule less than 2 cm in diameter, commonly located in a subcapsular location.

**M/C benign hepatic tumour Cavernous hemangioma M/C hepatic tumour in children Hepatoblastoma (Option B):** M/C Primary liver malignancy Hepatocellular carcinoma M/C cancer, which metastasis to the liver Colon carcinoma M/C sarcoma Angiosarcoma

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and signs of hypovolemic shock. She has a history of long-term contraceptive pill use. Imaging studies reveal a large hepatic mass with evidence of haemorrhage. Laboratory tests show elevated liver enzymes. What is the likely diagnosis based on her clinical presentation and medical history?

explanation.text: Based on the patients gender, history of use of OCP and clinical presentation, she most likely has a hepatic adenoma Hepatocellular adenoma is a benign neoplasm that typically occurs in young women. Strong association with the use of oral contraceptives Estrogen is known to promote the growth of hepatic adenomas by stimulating hepatocyte proliferation.
On imaging - well-circumscribed and encapsulated discrete mass, sometimes with associated hemorrhage - giving heterogenous appearance (fat+ hemorrhage).

The molecular subtypes of hepatic adenoma based on bordeaux classification are Hepatocyte nuclear factor 1-alpha ( HNF1α ) -inactivated hepatocellular adenoma which are multiple and presents in young patients Inflammatory hepatocellular adenoma - Most common to present with hemorrhage β-Catenin –activated hepatocellular adenoma

questions.question: A 25-year-old sexually active woman who has been on OCP for the past 4 years comes to the ER with severe abdominal pain and features of hypovolemic shock. Ultrasound reveals a large hemorrhagic hepatic mass and fluid in the peritoneum. What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanation.text: The risk of malignant depends on the molecular subtypes: (HNF1α)-inactivated hepatocellular adenoma- minimal risk Inflammatory hepatocellular adenoma - moderate risk β-Catenin–activated hepatocellular adenoma - high risk β-Catenin-–activated hepatocellular adenoma is strongly associated with OCP and anabolic steroid use.
Resection is recommended for β-catenin–activated tumours and tumours that are 5 cm or larger due to the risk of malignant transformation and haemorrhage.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions presents with a central stellate scar?

explanation.text: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia is a benign, non-neoplastic lesion which presents with a central stellate scar and is most common in women. It occurs due to altered blood flow, which causes hyperplastic changes in hepatocytes. It is usually asymptomatic and is incidentally seen on imaging.

questions.question: All of the following increases the risk of Hepatocellular carcinoma, except?

explanation.text: Gilbert's Syndrome is a benign condition associated with mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and does not cause liver damage or increase the risk of HCC. The most common risk factors are Viral infections (chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C) Toxic (Alcohol (Option A) and Aflatoxins) Metabolic (Diabetes and NASH (Option B), Hemochromatosis (Option C), Wilson's syndrome) Immune-related (Primary biliary cirrhosis and autoimmune hepatitis)

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the fibrolamellar variant of hepatocellular carcinoma?

options.A: Not associated with Hepatitis B, C

explanation.text: Fibrolamellar variant of hepatocellular carcinoma(HCC), where the malignant hepatocytes are separated by dense bundles of collagen is not associated with Hepatitis B, C Fibrolamellar variant Classical HCC Age Adolescents and young adults Older adults Gender Male=Female Male>Female Predisposing condition None Hepatitis B and C, Alcohol, NASH, Hemochromatosis AFP levels Normal (Option B) Increased Gene mutation DNAJB1-PRKACA TERT, Beta-catenin, TP53 Spread Lymphatic Hematogenous (Option C) Prognosis Good (Option D) Poor Serum markers Neurotensin B AFP, PIVKA II, Osteopontin, Glycipan 3, HepPar 1

questions.question: A patient with a longstanding history of alcoholism is admitted with jaundice, abdominal distension & weight loss. A liver biopsy done during his previous admission showed the following changes, and suspicion of malignant transformation is raised now. Elevation of which of the following markers will support the differential? HepPar-1 Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) Glypican-3 (GPC3) CA 15-3 Tissue polypeptide antigen

explanation.text: The following markers will be elevated in case of hepatocellular carcinoma: HepPar-1 (Statement 1) Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) (Statement 2) Glypican-3 (GPC3) (Statement 3) Neurotensin Arginase-1 CA-19-9 Chronic liver disease with cirrhosis is the major cause of transformation into hepatocellular carcinoma, and some of the common causes are listed below: Alcohol (as given in the above scenario) Chronic hepatitis B & C Metabolic diseases Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis Aflatoxins from Aspergillus

questions.question: A 2-year-old child presented with progressive jaundice for the past 2 months. Initial investigations were done, and subsequent histopathological examination of liver biopsy showed changes consistent with hepatoblastoma. Which of the following additional biomarkers will be elevated in this child?

explanation.text: Alpha-fetoprotein will be elevated in a patient with hepatoblastoma. Hepatoblastoma is the most common liver tumour of childhood. Activation of the Wnt signalling pathway is characteristic of hepatoblastoma, leading to nuclear β-catenin and increased expression of Wnt target genes such as glutamine synthetase in nearly all cases. It is important to note that elevated AFP is not pathognomonic to hepatocellular carcinoma.

Conditions where AFP is raised are listed below: Malignancy Non-malignant conditions Hepatocellular carcinoma Hepatoblastoma Secondary liver metastasis Nonseminomatous germ cell tumours Yolk sac tumour Neural tube defects Ataxia telangiectasia CA 19-9 and Neurotensin markers are elevated in Heptatocellular carcinoma. (Options A and C) CEA is a tumor marker for colorectal carcinoma. (Option D)
